Ayesha: Indu, it's been five hours. Want me to take the logs for a bit?
Indu: I've got it. Explaining would take longer than doing it.
Ayesha: Then at least sleep an hour. I'll page you.
Indu: No. Almost there 🙂
[two hours later]
Indu: oops
Indu: I ran the wrong command on the live database. It needs a restart from scratch.
Ayesha: Okay. Don't touch anything else. I'm calling the on-call lead now.
Indu: sorry. I should have handed over hours ago 😔
Ayesha: Send me exactly what you ran. We'll sort it.
[The site stayed down until morning.]

qa.a: Indu ran the wrong command on the live database.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling in the last messages?
qa.a: Indu felt regretful and embarrassed, apologising and admitting that a handover was due hours earlier. 😔

qa.q: What could Indu have done differently?
qa.a: Indu could have handed over the logs and rested, since a rested teammate might have caught the mistake or avoided it.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Indu turned down help?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably worried and a little sidelined, having offered twice and been refused.

grounding: Shows a senior engineer refusing help for hours until fatigue causes a wrong command that prolongs the outage.

subtype: Approach: hero engineer who refuses help [Pitfall]
passage:
The small internet provider in Haldwani lost service to three towns at 8 p.m. Arohi, the senior engineer who had built most of the network, sat alone at the router console. Ira, two years junior, pulled up a chair. 'Let me take the logs while you look at the configs.'
'I've got it,' Arohi said, without looking up.
At eleven, Ira offered again. At one in the morning, the manager called and asked if Arohi wanted a handover. 'Almost there.'
At 2.40, eyes red, Arohi typed a command meant for the backup router into the main one. The last working town, Bhimtal, went dark too. It was 6 a.m. before Ira and the manager, working together from fresh notes, brought everything back. The fix itself took twenty minutes once they looked at it with clearer eyes.

qa.q: What time did Arohi type the wrong command?
Why might Arohi have kept refusing help?
qa.a: Arohi likely felt proud and responsible for the network, and perhaps afraid that handing over would look like failure.

qa.q: What should have happened at eleven or at one?
qa.a: Arohi could have handed over to Ira or rested, since a tired mind makes mistakes like the 2.40 command.

qa.q: How might the people in Bhimtal have been affected?
qa.a: Their service, the last still working, went dark because of a tired mistake, stretching their outage until morning.

grounding: It shows a senior engineer refusing help for hours until fatigue leads to a wrong command that prolongs the outage.

subtype: Approach: hero engineer who refuses help [Pitfall]
passage:
In the Warsaw office, the hotel booking system went down at 5 p.m. on a Friday. Olga, who had written most of it, waved everyone off. 'Go home. I know this code better than anyone.' Esther stayed anyway and offered twice to take over the database side. Olga said no both times.
By midnight Olga had been awake for nineteen hours. She stopped posting updates in the channel; the manager only knew she was 'still on it'. At 2.15 a.m. she ran a cleanup meant for the test database against the live one. Two hours of new bookings vanished.
When the morning team arrived, they found Olga asleep at her desk and the outage twice as big. It took them until noon, and many emails to angry guests, to recover what they could.

qa.q: How long had Olga been awake by midnight?
What might Olga have been feeling when she waved everyone off?
qa.a: She seemed proud and certain, believing no one knew the code better, which made asking for help feel unnecessary.

qa.q: What approach could have prevented the 2.15 mistake?
qa.a: Accepting Esther's offer to split the work and handing over after a few hours, so a rested person made the risky changes.

qa.q: How might Esther feel in the morning?
qa.a: Esther may feel frustrated and sad, having offered help twice and watched the outage grow anyway.

grounding: It shows a senior engineer working alone for hours and refusing to hand over until fatigue leads to a wrong command that prolongs the crisis.
